title: Bloom Trading bot SOL drain
original_text:
if you keep SOL sitting in a Bloom trading bot wallet, treat it as exposed until there's a real post-mortem

@BloomTrading says 9 users lost ~9,408 SOL (~$947K) across 49 wallets, and blames a remote code execution bug in a third-party module. they say every other wallet is safe

what to do:
• move any balance you aren't actively trading to a wallet you control
• if you're one of the nine, only name your refund wallet through Bloom's official channels
• ignore every DM offering help or a refund. that's the next wave

the risk most ppl will miss: Bloom says no private keys were compromised. on a custodial bot that's not much comfort. their backend signs for you, so code running there doesn't need your key to move your funds

title: Strive 6,182 BTC buy funded by 15% SATS preferred
original_text:
ok so if you're reading Strive's 6,182 BTC buy as pure demand, look at what's paying for it

they spent $511.4M at ~$82,732 avg (Oct 17 to 23) and now hold 43,000 BTC. ppl are calling it two weeks of new supply absorbed by one company, and the math checks out

the part nobody's posting is the funding:
• it came off a $630M sale of SATS, a perpetual preferred paying 15% a year on $100, sold at $90
• that's ~$105M a year in dividends on the current shares, paid every business day from Nov
• they just opened a $1B ATM to sell more. fully sold, dividends go to ~$255M a year
• the company expects to pay those dividends mainly by raising more capital

and the full 43,000 BTC cost $3.8B ($87,785 avg). the prospectus marks it at $3.5B

my take: this isn't a holder, it's a pipeline. the bid lasts exactly as long as ppl keep buying 15% paper, and SATS last traded at $94.88, already under its $100 stated amount

so i'd watch SATS, not the BTC buys. if it slides toward $90, every new raise gets pricier and that bid gets a lot smaller

title: reply @AMLBotHQ Bloom Trading drain

title: Keystone authenticity key stolen, 18,835 devices destroyed
original_text:
if you got a Keystone hardware wallet delivered after oct 20, don't trust the authenticity check on its own anymore

new since the shipping data leak: @KeystoneWallet says the attacker also got the key that proves a device is genuine. it's burned in at manufacturing and can't be changed

• 18,835 devices in inventory with the old key get destroyed
• unshipped website orders are paused and moved to preorder
• 25,964 buyer records still held personal info (2024 to 2026 orders)
• seeds, private keys and the firmware signing key are not affected per Keystone

what to do:
• received before oct 20: Keystone says you're fine if it passes authentication. no need to move funds over this
• received after oct 20: contact support through Keystone's official authentication page and get it manually verified before loading funds
• ignore any recall or "send your device back" message. Keystone says it won't ask for returns

the risk most ppl will miss: that key's whole job is making a device look real. nobody's found a counterfeit yet, but a key that passes the check plus a list of buyers' home addresses is exactly the kit for mailing someone a fake "replacement"

title: Electrum RBF fee-bump theft, update to 4.8.3
original_text:
if you use Electrum on public servers and you're below 4.8.3, update before you send or fee-bump anything

a rogue server could hide your real payment, show you a fake pending one paying the attacker, then wait for you to bump the fee. the bump is what signs the theft

• attacker addresses matched the last 4 characters of the real recipient
• the fake tx had zero fee so it sat stuck, nudging you to RBF
• at least one confirmed loss. fix shipped oct 24 in 4.8.3
• users on their own self-hosted server weren't exposed

what to do:
• check Help > About, update to 4.8.3 from electrum.org only and verify the signature
• before any fee bump, check the full address and amount, on your hardware wallet screen if you use one
• don't trust a pending tx just because it shows in your history

the risk most ppl will miss: it's not only Electrum. BlueWallet's own fix PR says its fee-bump code has the same class of issue, and that fix isn't merged yet. if you're on BlueWallet, i'd hold off on fee bumps until it ships

title: Toros Options on Base routes through Derive
original_text:
ok so if you're reading Toros Options on @base as new onchain options liquidity, it's mostly the same book with a new front door

every trade routes through @DeriveXYZ's order book and market makers. @torosfinance just wraps each position as a token on Base, one option or a whole spread

• Derive does ~75% of onchain options notional per OAK Research
• Derive's builder codes let any frontend plug in and add its own fee
• DRV trading rewards were paused at the end of september
• Toros is paying 1% premium cashback at launch, no end date given

my take: this adds flow, not liquidity. spreads on Toros are only as tight as Derive's market makers, and their incentives just got cut

so i'd watch the HYPE and ZEC quotes once the cashback ends. that's where a thin book shows up first

title: Injective SICI GPU rental perps run on a 7-day average
original_text:
this matters if you're looking at @injective's new GPU rental perps: the index runs on a 7-day trailing average, not live prices

that lag is the whole game. a jump in rental prices today only bleeds into the index over the next week

• SICI basket: H100 40%, B200 25%, H200 15%, A100 10%, RTX 4090 10%
• priced hourly by London firm LO:TECH from compute marketplace listings, 19:00 UTC daily fixing
• each chip rebased to 100 at the july 22 fixing
• up to 10x leverage, USDC margin. no volume or OI numbers out yet

my take: the smoothing is great for hedgers and bad for anyone trading headlines. a GPU crunch won't show up as a candle, it shows up as a slow grind

i haven't confirmed the hourly readings are public. if they are, i'd watch the gap between the latest hourly basket and the 7-day average, because that gap tells you which way the index is already drifting

title: Tokenized stocks: AUM vs actual DeFi usage
original_text:
ok so if you're ranking tokenized stock issuers by AUM, you're mostly ranking tokens sitting in wallets doing nothing

per RedStone's late-september data, only ~2.6% of tokenized stock supply is used as DeFi lending collateral, even though ~42% is eligible

• Ondo: biggest issuer, $975M active value, 0.8% of it in DeFi
• xStocks: $365M, 27.2% in DeFi, and over half of all tokenized stock lending collateral
• Robinhood: $167M, 41.3% in DeFi
• DEX equity perps open interest hit $3.3B, more than the entire tokenized stock supply

my take: ppl want stock exposure onchain, but they want it as perps, not as tokens they lend out. the issuers are winning on AUM and losing on usage

so i'd watch which issuer gets real lending markets built around it next. that's what turns AUM into something DeFi can actually use

title: reply @KuCoin_AP xStocks DeFi usage
original_text: the stat that sets xStocks apart isn't the AUM, it's usage. RedStone's late-september data had about 27% of xStocks' active value in DeFi vs under 1% for Ondo, and xStocks alone was over half of all tokenized stock lending collateral

title: Foundation Passport phishing from official domains
original_text:
if you've ever bought a Passport from @FoundationHQ, assume the next "urgent" email about it is phishing

attackers used leaked Cloudflare API keys to send 23,000+ phishing attempts from Foundation's own domains, some reportedly with real names and shipping addresses. devices and funds are fine

don't click links in emails about your Passport, official domain or not
refund or replacement offers are bait
never type your seed phrase anywhere. if you already did, move to a new wallet with a new seed
final_text:
if you've ever bought a Passport from @FoundationHQ, assume the next "urgent" email you get might be a phishing email

exploiters used leaked Cloudflare API keys to send over 23k phishing emails from Foundation's own domains, some reportedly with users real names and shipping addresses

your devices and funds are fine, though it's of little consolation

just remember:
> don't click links in emails, official domain or not
> refund or replacement offers are bait
> never type your seed phrase anywhere

stay safe out there folks

title: bridge exploits end up as lender bad debt (Kelp)
original_text:
the bridge is where it started, but the lenders are the ones left holding it

kelp's rsETH bridge ran on a 1-of-1 verifier. one signature minted unbacked rsETH, which went straight into Aave to borrow real ETH

if your lending market takes bridged tokens as collateral, you're also betting on whoever secures that bridge

title: Bithumb + Coinbase vendor data leaks
original_text:

title: Solflare validator keys incident
original_text:
if you stake SOL with Solflare's validator, your SOL is safe but rewards are paused after their staking provider had the validator keys compromised

the migration will come through the Solflare app. any DM or link offering to "migrate" your stake before that is a scam
